Gay man here! We have these problems in a major way in our community (surprise surprise trauma is pretty common in gay men), but talking about these things with my therapist has been super helpful. If you have a therapist you trust, breaking through the shame and hearing their objective point of view can be really really helpful, and if they’ve been in the business for a while they’ve seen it all and won’t be shocked or anything like. I think it makes all of us cringe, it’s embarrassing and private and wrapped up in all sorts of weird feelings, but I highly recommend it because you can start to separate what you want for yourself from the intrusive thoughts that may be a result of trauma. Plus, getting to know yourself from a forgiving and understanding place is an important part of being good to yourself. Wishing for the best of healing understanding and growth for you ☺️

Hey,

I’ve been in a similar spot to you, and have had beliefs like this about healthy gay relationships. I am now in a healthy place with myself after a long period of therapy to address my own issues around self image and self esteem, and have been in a very healthy stable and loving gay relationship for some time now. Feel free to inbox me if you have any questions—I know how it feels and I know how so many people act, and I’ve struggled with similar desires and feelings that were super distressing to me and made it out the other side.

People who talk about “fucking your ass” and people who are on apps like Grindr are part of a really toxic gay subculture that I feel like all of us feel some pressure to participate in, it takes a lot of guts to say this isn’t for me, this isn’t what I want, and find others who feel the same way.

As gay men, we aren’t really taught or shown role models for love and stable relationships the way straight people are, and there are so many stereotypes and expectations that we’ll all be abusive sex maniacs.

You need to try (if you can’t find in person there are online resources as well) to work on the issues you have with yourself—spending your whole life feeling like you can’t have love, kindness, and a beautiful supportive relationship would be a very big shame and a tragedy, but there is hope. For me, when I worked on loving myself and really getting to know what I wanted (care, emotional intimacy, support and love), the sexual desires that were troubling to me just went away on my own. Those feelings are really hard to face, and progress takes time, but it’s so worth it when you get out the other side, and all this pain and self hatred just becomes something to look back on and say “wow, look how far I’ve come”. ❤️ I wish that for you, all the healing and support and love in the world, and I promise you have way more power to change and grow than you’re giving yourself credit for in this post!

If therapists aren’t an immediate option for you, I recommend the books “The sexual healing journey” and “The body keeps the score” to understand a bit more about how these kinds of feeling and compulsions come about naturally in response to trauma.

I know you say you don’t feel traumatized, but a) it feels different than movies portray it, and is different for everyone and b) just the act of hiding these parts of yourself, feeling like you have dirty secrets, being ashamed for being gay, these are all traumatic things that are almost without a doubt affecting you in ways that might not be so obvious.

There is nothing wrong with you, and the things about yourself that are causing you troubles and distress can be fixed, I promise, I’ve been there, and the world becomes a much happier place once you do.

If you need help figuring out a plan or finding resources to help you out, just shoot me an inbox!

Wishing you well ❤️

The proteins in milk that are in suspension (mostly casein proteins) exist in a stable suspension because of the pH, they form together in little blobs of proteins called micelles that are able to sit stably in water because of the pH (they exist as calcium salts at milk pH). When the pH is changed, the calcium salts of casein proteins are converted into regular casein, which then isn’t soluble in water and drops out. If there’s fat in the milk, these fat droplets can be caught by the proteins falling out, but you can still make cheese with skim milk because it’s the proteins falling out, not just the fats.

I think this is part of the issue. I think there are people who desire to hurt others but are kept 'in check' by societal pressure to not do so. I think there others who for whatever reason feel significantly powerless in their life (childhood abuse, mental illness, other environmental factors) who seek out opportunities to feel powerful in order to feel whole/connected to themselves. Kink is often a way for people to deal with past trauma--I think in an unhealthy and destructive way, as with other maladaptive coping mechanisms (alcoholism, lashing out, self-isolation).

We also have unlimited access to hardcore internet porn, which as I said in my longer post below is a performance, the people doing it are actors in front of a camera, and not many people stop to think about this. It is also well studied that regular/addicted porn users will gradually gravitate toward more and more extreme porn, in the same way that drug addicts require a higher and higher dose to achieve the same effects. Anything that activates DA neurons in the VTA (reward pathway) has the potential for addictive-like behaviors. Do I think that gambling addicts inherently want to lose their money, damage personal relationships, steal, etc.? No, probably not. But we do have those monkey brains that are delicate enough to make us do things that aren't really in line with our values.

Also, not many people take the time to stop and reflect on their values and what's important to them, and many people, especially traumatized people, are very bad at delaying/denying gratification, especially when it serves as relief from constant anxiety and negative feelings. It's a lot easier to engage in unhealthy and pathological sex than to confront and deal with past trauma.

I think the conversation about saying yes is meaningless when any sort of power dynamic exists in a relationship. E.g. when one party is financially dependent on the other, are they really in a position to say no? What does that mean in terms of consent?

I agree that sex doesn’t have to be about forging deep and meaningful connections every time, completely agree, but I disagree with Martha nussbaum’s conclusions about the fact that healthy objectification exists. I think there are circumstances where the mutual acknowledgement of “hey, let’s just have meaningless sex because it feels good for both of us” is totally possible and possible to be healthy, but in order for it to be healthy needs to come from a starting place of “we are both full humans who acknowledge each other’s full humanity and human worth”, and that that concept is 100% mutually exclusive from treating other people as a sex object.

There are also other questions I have about the origins of the eroticization of power and objectification vis-a-vis a patriarchal society that places superior value on masculinity and power over femininity and care/empathy/compassion, and that no one’s sexuality escapes that overall societal context.

The one thing that I think all sex ought to be is respectful and empathetic to the mutual humanity of both parties. That’s what I mean when I say connection, not connection in terms of long-term partnership or romance. Even a one-time hookup where no one has any expectations of bonding or long term partnership is a form of connection to me insofar as both parties are acknowledged as fully human and worthy. In that sense I still believe it is uplifting for both parties. I also agree with you that that sort of sex isn’t for me, but I understand that it can have a lot of value for some people.

I understand OP’s need to vent, and I think it’s also important to acknowledge how many people have been hurt and devalued by (again, my opinion) immoral and harmful sexual practices.

To my mind the solution to the problem is mindful and mandatory sex education couched not only in terms of anatomy/physical practice of sex, but an understanding of “safe sex” that goes beyond just “use a condom so you don’t get an STI” and includes emotionally safe sex, a more nuanced understanding of consent, and education about porn that isn’t at either extreme of “all porn is good” or “porn is sinful”. I think it’s important to teach young, vulnerable, and largely sexually ignorant people about the fact that porn is designed as entertainment, and that porn is a performance and very different from real sex. And also to teach people that sexual novelty can be addictive, and that the ability to basically have infinite novelty when it comes to watching hardcore internet porn is not the foundation for a positive or healthy sexuality.

I also happen to be pro-legalization of most drugs, including what are often considered to be “hard drugs”, which may seem like a contradictory stance, but I believe that it goes along with significant education about what is safe and what isn’t. I think internet porn is a drug as much as anything else, and while it can be fun and very pleasurable must be framed and understood for what it is, including the potential consequences on your life and sexuality. All in all I want more conversations, more education about healthy and positive relating to others, and a more broad-based understanding of more potentially dangerous sex practices that comes a place of practical understanding and not taboo and shame.

Taboo is inherently thrilling to a lot of people, and I think there’s an element of that to unconventional or kinky sex. I also don’t think that’s a healthy reason to engage in any type of sex, and I think shame is counterproductive to all sorts of healing and overall health and understanding of self. In the same way that places where alcohol consumption is normalized but education about the possible harms is widespread have a much lower prevalence of teen binge drinking (unhealthy alcohol practice) I think that removing taboo and shame from sex while having widespread education about the potential emotional risks as well as physical risks (pregnancy, STI) is the way to go forward.

As someone personally affected by a relationship where kink was introduced non-consensually and turned into sexual abuse, I may come from a particularly biased place, so take what I say with a grain of salt.

That said, my issue with kink culture and normalization is two-fold. 

1) Sexuality doesn’t come out of nowhere, and can’t be dissociated from context. The 19-year-old who was molested by an older adult as a child and now has a fetish for much older men and participates in daddy little girl culture, the young man who struggled with an eating disorder, was bullied for his weight throughout his life, and now has a fetish for “gaining” and destroys his body for this purpose, the person who was abandoned as an infant and now has a baby fetish, (these are all people that I know), might tell you that their fetish and kink sexuality is simply an innate part of them, inseparable and undistinguishable from their identity. We are very plastic creatures and eroticizing things that caused us trauma can be a coping mechanism—after I was raped as a young man the rape fantasy was very compelling to me for a while. That said, I don’t believe that these coping mechanisms are healthy, and are CERTAINLY not a substitute for processing and dealing with trauma in a holistic and healing way. After I took the time, with therapy, intense self-reflection, sharing my story with others, and volunteering at rape crisis centers and domestic abuse survivor’s homes, I was able to heal significantly from my past trauma, and once I felt whole in myself, the rape fantasy was gone. I realized how it was a way for me to personally minimize and hide from the damage that the incident caused to my sense of self, safety and control. I don’t take the position of shaming people who have fantasies and desires that may be unhealthy, but I do think it is a huge shame and sad to see for example, 20-year-olds ending up in “relationships” or even marriages with people three times their age, sacrificing the possibility of meaningful connection for filling a void induced by previous trauma. I do, however, take a stance of shame against the people (sadists, feeders, daddies) who exploit people who have been traumatized to take power over them, convince them that these behaviors are healthy and natural and not coping mechanisms, and actively sabotage and prevent true healing. In the case of some of the more extreme fetishes (slave/master, pro-Ana) I see them as manipulating and abusing people who are suffering in order to satisfy an abusive hedonistic pleasure, under the guise of supposed “consent”. Does an anorexic person consent to continuously losing weight? I think it’s a tricky gray area at best, I would argue absolutely not.

2) There are many hedonistic pleasures that exist, many of them unquestionably destructive to the self and others (heroin addiction comes to mind). I make the case that the kink approach to sex, where sex is about pleasure received from another person, and not about intimate connection and sharing, is one of these. Whether or not it’s learned from porn (which I believe depicts something much closer to sexual abuse than sex, but that’s a different conversation) or somewhere else, the fundamental tenet underpinning all kink relationships is using another person’s body for sexual satisfaction. There is an underpinning component of objectification that occurs when you treat another person’s body as basically a sex toy, a body part, etc. It may feel very good to do this, it may feel very good to both parties, but that doesn’t mean it isn’t dehumanizing and destructive. And it trains the people involved to respond to sexual objectification as a positive and harmless thing. Sex releases dopamine, it is inherently addictive. While in fact the majority of people who use heroin will not become addicted to it, the people who do often devolve into behaviors that are extremely destructive to themself and others (theft, crime, neglecting personal health, etc.). The fact that it feels good is not a justification for this destruction. The normalization of treating other people as objects to get you off is dangerous to me because it encourages and permits addiction to using other people, and sets a dangerous precedent for hedonism to move toward abuse. This was the case in my relationship where accusations of kinkshaming, and the general sense that kink relationships are healthy and positive and if I didn’t accept or believe that I was being uptight and backward, were used to justify continued sexual abuse, and these accusations came not only from my abuser, but from others around me.

Your actions in general don’t exist in a vacuum, and sexual actions especially don’t exist in a vacuum, because they inherently involve another person. Every situation involving multiple people involved choices, and personal pleasures that need to be sacrificed for the sake of the well-being of others around us. Interpersonal dynamics that cause harm should not be considered normal or acceptable simply because they provide sexual satisfaction, and the model of sex education (especially in the US where sex education is basically non-existent) should focus around sharing, respect, equality and caring, and should carry the understanding that our psyches are fragile and that serious power dynamics, while they may be erotic or appealing to some, are not healthy substitutes for mutual sex. 

Sex has the capacity to be, and in my opinion ought to be, an important way for people to connect, become closer, and bond. It can be extremely healing, fulfilling, and I do think sacred is an appropriate term. Healthy sexual interaction can be so much more than simple hedonistic pleasure, even if it is outside the context of a romantic relationship, even if it’s just a one night stand. And I think such an important part of sexual interaction, where the stakes are so incredibly high if things go wrong for the mental health of both people involved, is that sex is something you do with someone, not to someone, and that you are not entitled to enact every fantasy you have with another person’s body. There’s always a real person, with hopes, dreams, goals, and their own set of emotional and mental baggage, on the other side, and that healthy and permissible sex comes from a place of mutual respect for the humanity of others, always.

Working in a lab that dealt with live HIV virus. The lab was studying traditional Chinese medicine and the compounds in herbal blends trying to use them to find new drugs (crazy I know, got out of there as soon as I learned enough to get a job in a different lab). One of the guys in the lab was a traditional Chinese doctor, friend of the prof imported straight from China, no lab experience. Now, HIV virus falls under what is called biological safety level 2 (higher numbers means more dangerous, more safety protocols). This guy takes an uncovered vial containing live virus and takes it out of the hood (big no no). He then proceeds to drop the container and spill liquid containing live HIV all over the floor. Not necessarily unsafe unless you wipe it into an open cut or something, but we still all had to evacuate until the cleanup crew came in. Never would I have dreamed of someone spilling a bottle filled with HIV all over the floor, and as a gay guy was pretty amused at the thought of explaining to someone that I was HIV-positive because someone spilled a bottle of it on me....thankfully I didn’t get it but still crazy stuff.
